description: Finding elements on the page, changing them, and reacting to clicks and typing.

screens.body:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live map of your page: every heading, button, and input is an object JavaScript can find and change.

When your JS edits the DOM, the page updates instantly — no reload. That's how apps feel alive.

options: The browser's live, editable map of the page
check.question: What is the DOM?

screens.heading: The page is a tree you can touch
screens.keyPoint: The DOM = the page, as objects your code can change.

code.snippet:
// display-only: the DOM as a tree
document           // the whole page
  .querySelector("h1")  // find the main heading
  .textContent;         // read its text

screens.body:
document.querySelector("h1") finds the first h1 on the page. Pass a CSS selector — "#save-btn" finds the element with id="save-btn", ".card" finds the first element with class="card".

If you only ever learn one selection method, make it this one — it handles almost everything.

check.question: How do you select the element with id="save-btn"?

screens.heading: Selecting elements
screens.keyPoint: querySelector + a CSS selector finds nearly anything.

screens.body:
textContent reads or replaces an element's text. Assign to it and the page updates right away.

You can also tweak styles directly with element.style — handy for quick changes, though classes are cleaner for bigger styling.

check.question: How do you change an h1's text to "Welcome back!"?

screens.heading: Changing text and style
screens.keyPoint: textContent for words, style for quick looks.

screens.body:
An event is something that happens: a click, a keypress, a form submit. addEventListener wires your function to an event so it runs when the event fires.

Crucial detail: pass the function itself (handleClick), NOT the result of calling it (handleClick()). Parentheses = "run it now"; no parentheses = "run it on click".

check.question: Which correctly runs handleClick when the button is clicked?

screens.heading: Listening for events
screens.keyPoint: Pass the function — don't call it.

screens.body:
Your handler can receive the event object (usually called e). e.target is the element that was clicked — useful when one handler serves many buttons.

For forms, e.preventDefault() stops the page from reloading on submit, so your JavaScript can handle the data instead.

check.question: How do you stop a form submit from reloading the page?

screens.heading: The event object
screens.keyPoint: e.target = what was clicked. preventDefault = don't reload.

screens.body:
Inputs hold what the user typed in their .value property — always a string, even for number inputs.

Read .value when you need the data (on submit or on a button click), then validate it before using it.

check.question: How do you read what the user typed into an input?

screens.heading: Reading input values
screens.keyPoint: .value holds what the user typed — always a string.

screens.body:
classList.toggle("hidden") adds the class if it's missing and removes it if it's there — perfect for show/hide menus, dark mode, or marking items done.

You can also create elements from scratch with document.createElement and drop them into the page with appendChild.

options: It adds the class if missing, removes it if present
check.question: What does element.classList.toggle("hidden") do?

screens.heading: Toggling and creating elements
screens.keyPoint: toggle flips a class on/off — instant show/hide.
